```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
import os, sys, warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.ticker as mticker

def find_repo_root(start, name="CreditRiskLearning"):
    p = os.path.abspath(start)
    while True:
        if os.path.basename(p) == name:
            return p
        parent = os.path.dirname(p)
        if parent == p:
            raise FileNotFoundError(name)
        p = parent

REPO = find_repo_root(os.getcwd())
sys.path.append(os.path.join(REPO, "Core Resources"))
sys.path.append(os.path.join(REPO, "Core Resources", "Scripts"))

# Brand chart system + shared deck helpers (see Core Resources/Scripts/deck_utils.py)
from python_style_util import p, f, s, C
from credit_utils.eda import default_rate_by_bin
from deck_utils import (deck_style, BRAND_RAMP, add_baseline,
                        strip_bar_labels, small_labels, reset_labels)
deck_style()

DATA = os.path.join(REPO, "Datasets", "Home Credit Default Risk", "application_train.csv")
usecols = ["TARGET", "EXT_SOURCE_1", "EXT_SOURCE_2", "EXT_SOURCE_3",
           "DAYS_BIRTH", "DAYS_EMPLOYED", "NAME_EDUCATION_TYPE",
           "AMT_INCOME_TOTAL", "AMT_CREDIT", "AMT_ANNUITY", "AMT_GOODS_PRICE", "CODE_GENDER"]
df = pd.read_csv(DATA, usecols=usecols)
df = df[df["CODE_GENDER"] != "XNA"]
df["DAYS_EMPLOYED"] = df["DAYS_EMPLOYED"].replace(365243, np.nan)
df["AGE_YEARS"] = -df["DAYS_BIRTH"] / 365.25
df["EMP_YEARS"] = -df["DAYS_EMPLOYED"] / 365.25

def _sd(n, d): return n / d.replace(0, np.nan)
df["DTI"]          = _sd(df["AMT_ANNUITY"], df["AMT_INCOME_TOTAL"])
df["CREDIT_GOODS"] = _sd(df["AMT_CREDIT"],  df["AMT_GOODS_PRICE"])
df["EMPLOYED_AGE"] = _sd(df["DAYS_EMPLOYED"], df["DAYS_BIRTH"])

BASE = df["TARGET"].mean()
N = len(df)
```

## The short version {.hero data-kick="Executive summary"}

::: {.hero-wrap}
::: {.hero-col}
<div class="hero-num">~8%<small>of applicants hit repayment difficulty</small></div>
:::

::: {.hero-col}
Across **307,000+ applications**, a handful of signals separate that 8% cleanly:

- **External credit scores** — by far the strongest
- **Age & job tenure** — younger, less-tenured default more
- **Affordability ratios** — repayment size *relative* to the loan

And one thing that barely matters alone: **the raw loan amount**.
:::
:::

::: {.takeaway}
This deck is the *scan* — which fields carry signal — before any model is built. Every rate is read against the **8% base rate**.
:::

## The data in one slide {data-kick="The data"}

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.0
counts = df["TARGET"].value_counts(normalize=True).sort_index()
labels = ["Repaid on time", "Repayment difficulty"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.4))
bars = ax.barh(labels, counts.values, color=[p("jacaranda", 300), p("gold", 300)],
               alpha=0.95, edgecolor="white", linewidth=1.2, height=0.62)
for b, v in zip(bars, counts.values):
    ax.text(v + 0.012, b.get_y() + b.get_height()/2, f"{v:.1%}", va="center",
            fontweight="bold", fontfamily=f("mono"), fontsize=12, color=C.text)
ax.set_xlim(0, 1); ax.set_xlabel("Share of applications")
ax.set_title(f"{N:,} applications  ·  122 fields  ·  {BASE:.1%} hit repayment difficulty",
             loc="left")
ax.grid(axis="x"); ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.invert_yaxis()
plt.show()
```

::: {.takeaway}
The classes are **imbalanced** — roughly 12 good for every 1 bad. That's normal for credit, and it's why every group is read against the 8% line rather than a 50/50 split.
:::

## How to read a driver {data-kick="Method"}

For each field we sort applicants into bins (low → high) and check the **default rate in each bin** against the 8% base line.

- Bars that **slope** — the field separates good from bad → useful signal.
- Bars that stay **flat** on the line — no signal → drop it.

Colour just re-states height: [lighter = safer]{.stat}, the [deeper the purple]{.stat}, the higher the default rate.

::: {.takeaway}
That's the whole method. The next slides are this one chart, one field at a time.
:::

## Strongest signal — external credit scores {data-kick="Signal · strongest"}

```{python}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.3
fig, axes = default_rate_by_bin(
    df, ["EXT_SOURCE_2", "EXT_SOURCE_3", "EXT_SOURCE_1"],
    target="TARGET", ncols=3, bins=10, bin_label="rank",
    grade_scale=BRAND_RAMP, na_as_bin=True, panel_w=5.0, panel_h=4.7,
    show_base_rate=False,
)
add_baseline(axes, BASE)
plt.show()
```

::: {.takeaway}
A clean, steep slide from **~20% default in the lowest-score bin to ~2–3% in the highest**. These pre-built external scores are the single best predictors in the data.
:::

## Age & job tenure {data-kick="Signal · demographics"}

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
fig, axes = default_rate_by_bin(
    df, ["AGE_YEARS", "EMP_YEARS"], target="TARGET",
    ncols=2, bins=8, method="quantile", bin_label="range",
    grade_scale=BRAND_RAMP, na_as_bin=True, panel_w=6.4, panel_h=4.7,
    show_base_rate=False,
)
add_baseline(axes, BASE)
plt.show()
```

::: {.takeaway}
Both slope the intuitive way: **younger applicants, and those with less time in a job, default more**. Stability reads as lower risk. (The "missing" tenure bar is pensioners — correctly low-risk.)
:::

## Education tells a clean story too {data-kick="Signal · education"}

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.7
order = df.groupby("NAME_EDUCATION_TYPE")["TARGET"].mean().sort_values()
from matplotlib import colors as _mc
norm = _mc.Normalize(order.min(), order.max())
rgba = BRAND_RAMP(norm(order.values)); rgba[:, 3] = 0.95
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4.2))
bars = ax.barh(order.index.astype(str), order.values, color=rgba,
               edgecolor="white", linewidth=1.0)
ax.axvline(BASE, ls="--", color=C.text_muted, lw=1, zorder=1.4)
ax.text(BASE, len(order)-0.35, f" base {BASE:.1%}", va="bottom", ha="left",
        fontsize=11, color=C.text_muted, fontfamily=f("mono"), zorder=5,
        bbox=dict(facecolor="white", edgecolor="none", boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", alpha=0.85))
for b, v in zip(bars, order.values):
    ax.text(v + 0.002, b.get_y()+b.get_height()/2, f"{v:.1%}", va="center",
            fontweight="bold", fontsize=12, fontfamily=f("mono"), color=C.text)
ax.set_xlim(0, order.values.max() * 1.16)   # headroom so the top % label never clips
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mticker.PercentFormatter(xmax=1))
ax.set_title("Default rate by education level", loc="left")
ax.grid(axis="x"); ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
plt.show()
```

::: {.takeaway}
A steady gradient from **higher education (~2%) to lower secondary (~11%)** — education is a real, ordered driver.
:::

## The surprise — loan amounts barely matter {data-kick="Signal · the surprise"}

```{python}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.3
small_labels(9)   # denser bins -> smaller per-bar labels so they never touch
fig, axes = default_rate_by_bin(
    df, ["AMT_CREDIT", "AMT_INCOME_TOTAL", "AMT_ANNUITY"],
    target="TARGET", ncols=3, bins=10, bin_label="rank",
    grade_scale=BRAND_RAMP, panel_w=5.0, panel_h=4.7, show_base_rate=False,
)
reset_labels()
add_baseline(axes, BASE)
plt.show()
```

::: {.caveat}
As **raw amounts**, these are nearly flat — a big loan is not, by itself, a risky loan. The signal isn't the size; it's the size *relative* to income and the asset. That motivates the engineered ratios.
:::

## Engineered affordability ratios {data-kick="Feature engineering"}

```{python}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.3
fig, axes = default_rate_by_bin(
    df, ["EMPLOYED_AGE", "CREDIT_GOODS", "DTI"], target="TARGET",
    ncols=3, bins=12, bin_label="rank", grade_scale=BRAND_RAMP, na_as_bin=True,
    panel_w=5.0, panel_h=4.7, show_base_rate=False,
)
strip_bar_labels(axes)   # 12 near-equal bins -> labels collide; let the y-axis carry values
for ax in np.ravel(np.asarray(axes)):
    ax.margins(y=0.06)
add_baseline(axes, BASE)
plt.show()
```

::: {.caveat}
**Job-tenure share** and **loan-to-value** (`CREDIT_GOODS`) slope cleanly — the affordability signal the raw amounts lacked. But **debt-to-income (`DTI`) is flat**: the textbook metric underperforms here, almost certainly because self-reported income is noisy.
:::

## What we carry forward {data-kick="Shortlist"}

**Retained** as candidate drivers for the modelling screen:

- **External scores** (strongest), **age & tenure**, **education**
- **Affordability ratios** — loan-to-value and tenure-share
- Weak-but-documented: DTI / income ratios (kept to *show* they underperform)

**Deliberately parked** (reversible, one line to re-add):

- Social-circle and bureau-enquiry counts — too weak to earn a baseline slot

::: {.takeaway}
A **lean, defensible shortlist** beats a kitchen sink — it's the judgment call, not the field count, that matters.
:::

## Caveats & what's next {data-kick="Caveats · next"}

- **Gender is excluded** from any model — responsible-lending / anti-discrimination — and used for context only.
- The model **leans heavily on opaque external scores**; self-reported income is noisy.
- Application-time data only; **missing values are kept as their own group** where the absence is itself informative.

::: {.caveat}
**Next:** turn this scan into a ranked screen (WOE / Information Value), then a first interpretable scorecard. This deck answers *"what looks predictive"*; the next answers *"how strongly, and in what order."*
:::
